SOURCE: "AIOS: LLM Agent Operating System", Kai Mei, Xi Zhu, Wujiang Xu, Mingyu Jin, Wenyue Hua, Zelong Li, Shuyuan Xu, Ruosong Ye, Yingqiang Ge, Yongfeng Zhang (Rutgers). Header: "Published as a conference paper at COLM 2025"; arXiv:2403.16971v5 [cs.OS], 12 Aug 2025 (first arXiv March 2024; file name says 2024).

COVERAGE: all 34 of 34 pages read, text extracted in full (105431 chars), including the appendices (A kernel, B SDK, C benchmarks, D extra results, E discussion). Skimmed: the reference list. Figures 6-8 and 10-15 are bar and line charts with no numeric labels. I read only the axes and captions, so I give no per-framework numbers for them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: AIOS gives up to 2.1x higher throughput when serving agents from several frameworks.
  number: 2.1x (the abstract says "faster execution", Sec 4.3 says throughput)
  setup: Reflexion agents on Llama-3.1-8b, HumanEval, one A5000 24GB GPU, a single LLM that handles one prompt at a time, up to 250 concurrent agent threads, RR scheduling, float16. This is the best case. The other frameworks gain less (shown only in the bar charts).
  quote: "AIOS achieves significantly higher throughput across different agent frameworks, to a 2.1× increase in throughput when using Reflexion-based agents on Llama-3.1-8b."
  where: p8, Sec 4.3
- claim: The paper attributes the speedup to scheduling that avoids the trial-and-error GPU loading seen in existing frameworks. It does not test this explanation in isolation.
  number: none
  setup: The framing is that Autogen and LangChain call the LLM concurrently and retry after CUDA out-of-memory exceptions.
  quote: "This improvement is attributed to the scheduling employed in the AIOS kernel, which prevents unnecessary trial-and-error attempts by avoiding prompts that cannot be loaded onto the GPU for execution."
  where: p8; the baseline description is on p2
- claim: In the scheduler ablation, FIFO and RR roughly halve overall time compared with no AIOS. FIFO is faster on average. RR has the better p90 wait.
  number: None 152.1 s overall, avg wait 9.8, p90 11.0; FIFO 74.2, 3.0, 5.0; RR 77.3, 3.2, 4.2
  setup: ReAct agents, HumanEval, Llama-3.1-8b. This is a single configuration and the paper gives no variance.
  quote: "None 152.1 9.8 11.0 / FIFO 74.2 3.0 5.0 / RR 77.3 3.2 4.2" and "RR performs better on the p90 metric ... due to its fairer scheduling approach, which reduces the likelihood of later tasks having longer waiting time, which can typically occur in FIFO."
  where: p31, Table 6 and Sec D.1
- claim: Agent benchmark success rates stay the same or rise slightly with AIOS. Gains are small.
  number: HumanEval ReAct 48.8 to 50.6; MINT ReAct 29.4 to 30.1; GAIA ReAct 5.5 to 7.3; SWE-Bench-Lite ReAct 3.9 to 4.3; GAIA Autogen 7.3 to 9.7; MINT Open-Interpreter 45.9 to 48.7. Autogen HumanEval, MINT and SWE-Bench-Lite are unchanged (87.8, 42.5, 4.3). MetaGPT HumanEval and SWE-Bench-Lite are unchanged (82.9, 5.9).
  setup: GPT-4o-mini as the LLM core, temperature 1.0, success rate (SR%). Single runs, no confidence intervals. GAIA is "-" for Open-Interpreter and MetaGPT because of missing API support.
  quote: "ReAct w/o AIOS 48.8 29.4 5.5 3.9 / ReAct w/ AIOS 50.6 30.1 7.3 4.3"
  where: p7, Table 1
- claim: The authors explain the accuracy gains by two mechanisms, prompt enhancement and tool-call validation. They do not ablate either.
  number: none
  setup: Code benchmarks get structured system prompts inside the LLM wrapper. GAIA gets regex pre-execution parameter validation of tool calls and a hashmap that resolves concurrent tool conflicts.
  quote: "AIOS boosts agent performance by prompt enhancement, which embeds the system prompts with more structural input and output within the LLM wrapper." and "pre-execution parameter validation via structural regex to check the format of tool calls before execution, and (2) conflict resolution hashmaps to mitigate concurrent access issues."
  where: p8, Sec 4.2
- claim: Scaling is roughly linear from 250 to 2000 agents. The gap to the no-AIOS baseline widens as agent count grows.
  number: 250 to 2000 agents; 164 HumanEval samples duplicated to reach the counts; y-axis range 200 to 1000 s execution time and 2.5 to 17.5 s mean wait (read from the axes of the figure)
  setup: Llama-3.1-8b and Mistral-7b on HumanEval
  quote: "AIOS maintains approximately linear relationships between both overall execution time and average agent waiting time relative to agent count."
  where: p8-9, Fig 8
- claim: Architecture. Agent queries are decomposed into syscalls (LLM, memory, storage, tool). Each syscall is bound to a thread and dispatched by a central scheduler that holds all the queues. The kernel has three layers (application, kernel, hardware) with separate modules.
  number: none
  setup: The scheduler supports FIFO and Round Robin. Appendix A.3 says priority-based schedulers can be derived from BaseScheduler, but only FIFO and RR are evaluated.
  quote: "We centralize all queues within the scheduler module rather than distributing them across processing modules, isolating request management responsibilities and allowing each module to focus solely on execution."
  where: p3-4, Sec 3.1 and 3.3
- claim: The context manager snapshots and restores a partially finished LLM generation, so RR time slices do not lose work. There is a text-based variant for closed APIs and a logits-based variant that keeps beam-search state. The authors report no output loss.
  number: BLEU 1.0 and BERT score 1.0, for both text-based and logits-based methods
  setup: Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B (Table 7 prints "Llama-3-8B", while the main text uses Llama-3.1-8b), context switch on versus off, same agent and conditions
  quote: "both BLEU and BERT scores achieve a value of 1.0."
  where: p4-5 (Sec 3.4); p32 (Table 7); p31 (Sec D.2)
- claim: The memory manager keeps per-agent memory in RAM and evicts to disk by LRU-K once usage passes a threshold. The storage manager adds a vector DB, file versioning, locks and rollback.
  number: 80% of the memory block (configurable); max_versions=20
  setup: Design description only, with no evaluation of memory or storage.
  quote: "When an agent's memory usage exceeds its block limit (e.g., 80% of allocation), the memory manager initiates a K-Least Recently Used (LRU-K) eviction policy"
  where: p5, Sec 3.5; p19-20, A.5-A.6
- claim: The tool manager validates parameters before execution. For tools with parallel-access limits it keeps a per-tool instance counter. When a request would exceed the limit, it skips ahead in the queue to the next request that does not conflict.
  number: none
  setup: Design only.
  quote: "upon detecting conflicts, the system advances to subsequent queue requests until identifying a conflict-free candidate."
  where: p6, Sec 3.7
- claim: The access manager has privilege groups held in a hashmap from agent ID to group, and it asks the user to confirm irreversible operations. It guards cross-agent data access, not tool-call authorization generally.
  number: none
  setup: Design only. There is no security evaluation or attack test.
  quote: "This mandates explicit user verification before proceeding with potentially destructive operations on files or tools."
  where: p6, Sec 3.8; p21, A.8
- claim: The SDK adapts existing frameworks by monkey-patching their LLM-call functions, so agent code does not change. The adapters cover ReAct, Reflexion, Autogen (0.2 only), Open-Interpreter and MetaGPT. The SDK ships 17 native tools.
  number: 17 tools
  setup: Per the paper, SDK calls reach the kernel as HTTP requests to localhost or a remote URL through send_request().
  quote: "The SDK incorporates 17 native tools spanning multiple modalities and functionalities"
  where: p6-7, Sec 3.9; p22-29, App B

LIMITS
- The authors concede few limits. The Future Directions section (App E.2) lists the gaps: semantic and dependency-aware scheduling, faster and compressed context snapshots, shared memory and storage between agents, and safety and privacy hardening. Its safety items are jailbreaking, unauthorized access to another agent's memory, encryption and watermarking. These are not implemented or tested.
- The workload is narrow. One GPU, one LLM serving one prompt at a time, and benchmarks that are mostly single-agent coding. There is no multi-LLM or multi-GPU test, no heterogeneous workloads, and no agents with real long-running tool use. The throughput gain depends on the baseline's retry-on-CUDA-OOM behaviour, so it may shrink against batching servers such as vLLM. The paper does not compare against those.
- The efficiency charts are normalized and carry no printed values. Benchmark deltas are single runs with no variance. Several of the gains are 0.3 to 1.8 points.
- The accuracy-gain explanations (prompt enhancement, regex validation) are asserted and not ablated. The prompt-enhancement effect is confounded with the system itself.
- Nothing tests the access manager, the memory manager or the storage manager. There is no measurement of LRU-K, RAM-to-disk swap or user-intervention behaviour.
- The paper's own taxonomy puts the benchmarked agents' scheduling work in the kernel, not in agent orchestration (planning, handoff, multi-agent topology). Orchestration of agent logic stays in the adapted frameworks. AIOS only provides resource scheduling beneath them.
- Dated: models are Llama-3.1-8b, Mistral-7b and GPT-4o-mini. Autogen 0.2 only is supported. Check the repo for later changes.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Classic OS ideas: time-sharing (Ritchie & Thompson, 1974), multitasking (Hoare, 1974; Engler et al., 1995, exokernel), process scheduling (Liu & Layland, 1973; Dijkstra, 2002), memory management (Denning, 1968; Daley & Dennis, 1968), filesystems (Rosenblum & Ousterhout, 1992; McKusick et al., 1984).
- Agent frameworks it adapts: ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), Autogen (Wu et al., 2023), Open-Interpreter (Lucas, 2024), MetaGPT (Hong et al., 2023).
- Its own earlier vision paper: Ge et al. 2023b, "LLM as OS, Agents as Apps: Envisioning AIOS, Agents and the AIOS-Agent Ecosystem" (arXiv:2312.03815). Also Ge et al. 2023a, OpenAGI.
- Benchmarks: HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MINT (Wang et al., 2023b), GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), SWE-Bench-Lite (Jimenez et al., 2024).
- Beam search is the basis of the logits-based snapshot. LRU-K is cited without a named reference.

CODE
- p15: the syscall thread binding, "class SysCall ( Thread ) : def __init__ ( self , agent_name , request_data ) : ... self . event = threading . Event () ... self . pid = None ... self . time_limit = None" and "def run ( self ) : self . set_pid ( self . native_id ) ; self . event . wait ()". Each syscall is its own thread, blocked on an event until the scheduler releases it.
- Appendix A.3, p17: BaseScheduler has per-type process_llm_requests, process_memory_requests, process_storage_requests and process_tool_requests loops, plus start() and stop().
- Appendix A.4, p17-18: SimpleContextManager.generate_response_with_interruption(..., pid, time_limit, ...) -> Tuple[Any, bool], with load_context(pid) and clear_context(pid).
- Appendix A.8, p21: AccessManager.add_privilege(sid, tid); check_access(sid, tid); ask_permission(operation).
- Appendix A.6, p20: StorageManager(root_dir, use_vector_db=True, max_versions=20), with sto_rollback(file_path, n=1, time=None).
- Appendix B.5, p28-29: the decorator pattern @add_framework_adapter("AutoGen ~0.2") for patching OpenAIWrapper.create and ConversableAgent methods.
- Appendix B.1, p23: Query base class with query_class: Literal["llm","memory","storage","tool"], and LLMQuery.action_type in {chat, chat_with_json_output, chat_with_tool_call_output, call_tool, operate_file}.

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p2: a travel agent's 7 steps, split between LLM-managed services and OS-managed services. It motivates the kernel split.
- Fig 2, p3: the three-layer architecture with the kernel modules. This is the main overview diagram.
- Fig 3, p4: how agent queries decompose into syscalls, are thread-bound, and go to per-module queues in the scheduler. Best for the orchestration note.
- Fig 4, p5: logits-based context snapshot and restore with beam width 1, using the "weather in Paris" example.
- Fig 5, p6: memory-to-storage eviction at the 80% limit.
- Fig 6-7 (p8), 10-15 (p31-34): normalized throughput and latency per framework, benchmark and model. No printed values.
- Fig 8, p9: execution time and wait time against 250-2000 agents.
- Fig 9, p23: the SDK send_request path from agent code to the kernel over HTTP.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- Extraction was clean. Code blocks and figure text have broken spacing, such as "Determinewhethertherewillbe", but the numbers are intact.
- The abstract says "2.1× faster execution". The body measures a 2.1x throughput increase, not wall-clock time. For wall-clock, Table 6 shows about 2.0x (152.1 to 74.2 s, ReAct on Llama).
- Sec 4.2 describes the tool-call validation as "two following mechanisms", but the numbering in the extraction is garbled ("(2)" appears without a "(1)").
- Table 7 says Llama-3-8B, but Sec 4.1 says Llama-3.1-8b.
- The 2.1x figure and the "up to" in the abstract come from one cell. Per-framework values are only in charts.
